title: AI robots are roaming L.A. grocery aisles. Shoppers and workers worry about what comes next
key_facts: Simbe Robotics' Tally, a six-foot tower of sensors, now rolls through aisles at Ralphs and other Los Angeles-area grocery stores to find low, out-of-stock or misplaced items.

Simbe says more than 3,000 of its robots are contracted to monitor shelves worldwide; Kroger, Ralphs' parent, uses hundreds, and a store manager's LinkedIn post said it deployed its 500th robot in August.
Simbe says Tally "is designed to understand shelf conditions, not identify or track humans" and can save employees up to 50 hours of work per week.
Unions worry about job losses: UFCW Local 770 president Kathy Finn said members should not learn of major changes "only after new technology shows up in their stores".
A Ralphs employee, Rachel Fournier, said the robots "just showed up out of nowhere"; a shopper said she would shop elsewhere to avoid more automation.
Kroger said this week it will lay off 3,000 corporate employees over three years as it uses more AI, but the paper notes those are not inventory jobs.
Fortune Business Insights estimates the retail automation market could grow from $28 billion in 2025 to $77 billion by 2034.

why_it_matters_hint: Shelf-scanning robots are quietly arriving in everyday shops, and workers fear lost hours and monitoring even though retailers say the machines free staff for other tasks.
